originalTitle: Trump backs Pete Hegseth amid renewed tensions with Iran – live
summary: Trump said he thinks his defense secretary ‘has done a great job’
content: A controversial move by the Pentagon to reclassify casualties in the Iran war is being taken by US military veterans as a sign of disrespect for the dead. “It’s such a huge disrespect for the families,” said Michael E Smith, a retired US rear admiral and the founder of National Security Leaders for America. “To claim that they weren’t killed as a result of the war – oh, it was just overseas operations – is just ludicrous.” In a quiet weekend update to the Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS), a military database for displaying casualties, the US Department of Defense – renamed the Department of War under Donald Trump – added more than 140 wounded service members. They also introduced a new casualty category labeled “Overseas Operations” for personnel killed and wounded “starting July 7” which splits the count from the beginning of the US-Israel war on Iran. Four US service members killed in action by Iranian forces fall under that category: 1st Lt Tyler James Feehan, Pvt Isabella Gonzales, Sgt Angel S. Rampersad and Sgt Michael Emmanuel Swinton. “I definitely think that this isn’t an issue just about numbers, but also about accountability,” said Tristeza Ordex, a US Marine Corps veteran and the national organizer of partnerships and engagement at VoteVets. “When I was deployed to Afghanistan, I remember attending ramp ceremonies,” she said, referring to an airfield memorial honoring a fallen service member before their casket is loaded onto an aircraft and returned home. The Michigan Senate debate, which raced by at lightening speed, closes with this question from the moderator: “We have 30 seconds left for each of you to answer the following question: what makes you think you’re the formidable candidate who can take on Mike Rogers?” “Poll after poll after poll,” El-Sayed begins, “has shown, despite what my colleague says, that I am the most competitive candidate to take on Mike Rogers.” “But it’s also this that you’ve got to have something you’re fighting for,” he continues. “Ask yourself, if DTE funds both Mike Rogers and Haley Stevens, who wins?” El-Sayed asks, referencing donations from Detroit-based DTE Energy which provides power to Southeast Michigan customers. “DTE wins and Blue Cross and Big Pharma and Big Tech and Aipac: all funded by the same people,” he answers. “We need a choice. I’m the only candidate in this race who does not take corporate money. And so I offer a real contrast to a guy who has never seen a corporate dollar he did not want,” El-Sayed concludes. “Well, look,” Stevens says. “Governor Whitmer, attorney general Nessel, the chair of the Michigan legislative Black caucus, Amos O’Neill, they all agree that I will be Michigan’s workhorse, that I will stand up for us on day one, that I will beat Mike Rogers, just like I have beat Republicans four times over.” With that, the debate ends, a week before Democratic primary voters pick one of the two to try to hold the US Senate seat being vacated by retiring Democratic senator Gary Peters. Democrats know that they need to retain the seat to have any realistic chance of regaining control of the Senate in November. “Anybody who knows me, knows that getting people health care is the passion of my life,” El-Sayed says, when asked about his main goal in seeking office. “I went to medical school only to realize that too often our health care system is part of the problem.” “We need and deserve guaranteed health care through Medicare for All,” he continues. “I have been thinking about this question. In fact, I’ve testified to the US Senate twice.” “Now on Medicare for All, there is work that we’re going to have to do,” he adds. “We’re going to have to get a president elected who can do it in 2029. Now, in the process, though, I actually think that we could eliminate all the medical debt in this country, $225b.” “Complaints and slogans aren’t solutions,” Haley Stevens says in an extended discussion of which candidate’s approach to stopping the abuses of ICE is more effective. “I went up to an ICE detention facility to call out and see why people were losing their lives, why they were being held for long periods of time without due process. This has been an outrage,” Stevens says. “Look, a lot of you remember Abdul from when he first ran for governor in 2018,” she continues, turning back to her frame that her opponent is more experienced as an influencer than a lawmaker. “It didn’t work out, so he started the podcast, he wrote the books, and now he’s running for Senate and he’s already bought the website for president. You know, it’s just another rung on the ladder.” “That’s not what this job is for me,” Stevens adds. “That’s not why I’m putting up my hand in this moment. It’s not about celebrity. This is about making sure that Mike Rogers doesn’t get anywhere close to this seat. I’m the only one on this stage who has beat MAGA four times”. “Like I told all the viewers at the outset that while my opponent was going to make this about me and her, I want to make this about you somehow,” El-Sayed counters. “Congresswoman, if you enjoy podcasts about public health, I welcome you to take a listen. You seem very concerned about that. I’m more concerned about the fact that people can’t pay for their gas. They can’t pay for their groceries. We’re fighting a war that’s cost us billions of dollars, that has been pushed by the the government of a foreign country, the same foreign country that the folks paying for your ads want us to send billions of dollars to.” In response to a question about ICE, Stevens damns El-Sayed with faint praise, saying: “I am standing up to Trump right now on these abuses of power, not shouting into a bullhorn, not getting in front of the first camera I see, but doing the hard work. That is what Michigan deserves. Look my my opponent here, Abdul, he is such a talented guy. He’s written three books. He did 300 podcasts. You know, he’s had all this attention.
